newsitem.title: UK: UK Stonehenge plan dashed by lottery fund rejection.
newsitem.headline: UK Stonehenge plan dashed by lottery fund rejection.

text.p: Plans for badly-needed improvements to the site of Britain's biggest tourist attraction, the prehistoric monument of Stonehenge, were dashed on Friday when the site's operators were refused funds from the national lottery.

The decision by the Millenium Commission, one of the bodies which distributes lottery funds, means that a 43 million pound ($70 million) plan to expand the site of the mysterious, 5,000 year-old monument in southwest England and build a high-tech visitor centre will have to be abandoned.
"We are extremely disappointed," said a grim-faced Sir Jocelyn Stevens, chairman of English Heritage, announcing the news.
There was no immediate comment from the Millenium Commission on the reasons for the decision.

Stevens said he believed part of the reason for the commission's decision was its unhappiness with the private financing of part of the project by Tussauds Group, part of the Pearson media and leisure group.
"I was led to believe the Millenium Commission was discomfited by the private finance element because it involved a profit," he told a news conference.

Tussauds had agreed to invest 10 million pounds in the project and to operate the visitor centre which would explain the history of Stonehenge and the many other prehistoric monuments around the site.
Although entry to Stonehenge, its surrounding area and the car park would be free, Tussauds had planned to make its profit from entrance fees to the centre, a spokesman said.
Under the plan, one of the roads running near to Stonehenge would have been closed and grassed over and it was hoped another would be hidden by a tunnel.
Neither was now likely to happen, Stevens said.

"Stonehenge is one of the greatest prehistoric monuments in Europe and possibly the world, receiving one million visitors per year. Research shows that over half find the experience very disappointing," he said.
A recent Rough Guide to Britain agreed.

"Instead of being encouraged to let their imaginations rip, visitors have to put up with being funnelled through a tunnel under the A344 (road) and then staring at the stones from behind a barbed-wire barricade with a constant backdrop of roaring traffic," the guide's authors wrote.

Stonehenge is a circle of giant stones, dating from about 2,800 BC, which stand on their ends. Some still have huge stone lintels lying across the top and an "altar stone" at the open northeast side of the circle faces the rising sun.
It has become a sacred place for mystical "druids" who are fighting for the right to celebrate the summer and winter solstices there.
Historians know little about how it was built or who built it. There are also another 400 barrows -- ancient burial mounds -- scattered around the site on Salisbury Plain. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
